query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high‐throughput, calibrated differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) protocol—implemented with a modulated heating schedule and coupled in situ with dilatometry—can accurately and efficiently measure the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and other liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across a representative set of high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), providing results comparable to or better than conventional, separate techniques.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase high‐entropy alloys in the solid solution state, covering a range of compositions from the HEA family.
generation.intervention: Implement a combined high‐throughput DSC measurement with modulated temperature ramp and simultaneous in situ dilatometry. The DSC is calibrated using reference materials with known phase transformation properties, ensuring that the latent heat and baseline corrections are accurately determined, while dilatometry captures the volume change at melting.
generation.conditions: Experiments are conducted under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The temperature is ramped from room temperature to above the melting point at controlled rates (with variable heating rates tested to isolate kinetic effects). The measurements are performed on small, well‐characterized HEA samples with their compositions defined, and with calibrations made using standard metals or alloys of known thermal properties.
generation.structural_mediator: The sharp stage transition at melting manifests as an endothermic peak in the DSC signal and as an abrupt volumetric expansion in dilatometry, which serve as mediators for extracting the liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties.
generation.mechanism: During the DSC measurement, the precise control and modulation of the heating profile permit a clear deconvolution of the latent heat (enthalpy) from background contributions. Integration of the DSC endotherm yields the enthalpy of fusion; differentiation with respect to temperature, when combined with the latent heat value, provides the entropy of fusion. In situ dilatometry simultaneously records the volume change that occurs at the phase transition, linking the thermochemical signature to structural expansion. Together, these measurements yield a comprehensive set of melting characteristics that can be related via established thermodynamic relations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to traditional separate DSC and dilatometry measurements, the integrated high‐throughput approach is expected to determine the melting temperature within a narrow uncertainty (on the order of a few percent) and measure fusion enthalpy and entropy with uncertainties comparable to state‐of‐the‐art methods. The measured volume change at melting will follow the expected trends based on compositional variations in HEAs, and the liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties will exhibit a smooth, continuous dependence across the family.
generation.baseline: Conventional thermal analyses using standard DSC and separate high‐temperature dilatometry serve as the baseline methods for determining these thermodynamic properties in simpler alloy systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to HEAs that are single‐phase solid solutions up to their melting point. Its efficiency and accuracy may be limited if secondary phases or chemical reactions (e.g., oxidation) occur near the melting region, or if extreme kinetic limitations affect the DSC signal.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties mainly arise from calibration precision, baseline subtraction errors, and heating rate–dependent kinetic effects. It is expected that these uncertainties can be controlled to within ±5% for enthalpy and ±2% for melting temperature for high‐quality samples; however, for alloys that exhibit atypical behavior (e.g., wide melting intervals), additional calibration or data deconvolution may be needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of HEAs covering a range of compositions within the targeted family. Perform the integrated DSC–dilatometry measurements under the specified controlled conditions and record the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting. Independently, subject the same samples to conventional calorimetry and high‐temperature density measurements (or drop calorimetry) as benchmarks.
measurements: DSC endotherm peak temperature and integrated heat flow
Conventional calorimetric and density measurement data for each sample
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated method fails to reproduce the melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change within the expected uncertainty limits (e.g., deviations greater than ±10% compared to the benchmark methods), or if the data do not exhibit the expected continuous compositional trends, then the proposed approach will be refuted.
